ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Denver, CO
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Denver area refining, pipelines, mining and steel fabrication, done on your site. Request a UT quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Denver, Colorado
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld inspection for Denver-area owners: wall surveys on refinery piping and vessels, gathering-system and flowline steel, mining equipment wear parts, and groove welds on fabricated structures. Technicians are mobilized to your site with calibrated equipment, examine to a written procedure, and report against the code you name. Request a UT quote for your Denver scope and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used around Denver

Denver's industrial work is spread along the Front Range and out into the mountain states rather than concentrated on one waterfront. Oil and gas operators in the Denver-Julesburg Basin run wellhead flowlines, gathering systems, compressor stations and processing plants. The refinery at Commerce City has process piping and vessels on the usual corrosion-monitoring programs. Metal fabrication shops, equipment manufacturers and aerospace suppliers sit across the metro, and mining operations in the mountain west maintain heavy steel structures and wear parts.

The ultrasonic jobs that follow from that mix:

  • Thickness at risers, bends, low points and tie-ins on gathering lines and production piping, where wall loss concentrates where water settles.
  • Condition monitoring locations on refinery piping, exchangers and vessels, fed into the owner's remaining-life calculations.
  • Girth welds and tie-in welds on new pipe, and repair welds on existing lines, examined with a shear-wave technique where the owner's procedure allows.
  • Shell and floor thickness on aboveground storage tanks at terminals and production facilities.
  • Wear plates, chute liners, mill shells and boom structure on mining and aggregate equipment.
  • Groove welds on fabricated steel structures, including bridge and building steel, examined to the structural welding code.

What ultrasonic testing finds, and what it misses

Straight-beam thickness measurement sends sound through the wall and times the echo from the back surface. On corroded steel, dual-element probes are preferred because the separate transmitting and receiving crystals cope better with a rough exterior. The reading describes the wall at that spot only. Corrosion under a flowline's coating or inside a tank bottom can be patchy, so a sparse set of points can pass over the worst area. The grid, the choice of locations and the repeatability of each location matter more than the number of decimal places on the display.

Angle-beam examination sends a shear wave into a weld and looks for lack of fusion, cracks and slag, flaws that a surface method cannot reach. Both techniques have limits: heavy scale and rough coating disturb coupling, cast and coarse-grained steel scatters sound, lamination can hide the back wall, and a pitted wall can mislead a digital readout that locks onto the wrong echo, so a waveform display is preferred where pitting is suspected. UT reports wall and flaw geometry; it does not explain the damage mechanism, which belongs to the owner's engineer.

Codes and Colorado requirements

Technique documents are ASME Section V Article 4 for weld examination, Article 5 for material examination and Article 23 with SE-797 for contact thickness measurement, and ASTM E797 and E164 cover the corresponding practices. Process piping under ASME B31.3 uses paragraph 344.6 and Table 341.3.2 for acceptance, and pressure vessels under Section VIII Division 1 use Mandatory Appendix 12. Structural steel follows AWS D1.1 including ultrasonic acceptance for groove welds, while state transportation steel follows AWS D1.5. Pipeline girth welds follow API 1104, and its provisions apply to whatever examination method the owner's procedure selects.

In-service equipment adds API 510, 570 and 653, under which the owner's authorized inspector is responsible and Atlantis supplies the examination data. Atlantis is not the inspector of record. Colorado adds its own layers. The Energy and Carbon Management Commission administers flowline regulations in its 1100 series, with an Integrity Group that reviews flowlines, audits operators using a ranking model and checks pressure-testing records, and operators must supply data on line diameter, fluid and material. The Colorado Department of Labor and Employment's Division of Oil and Public Safety runs the boiler inspection program, which covers boilers and some pressure vessels in commercial and public buildings, using state inspectors or commissioned insurance inspectors. Federal PHMSA rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 apply to jurisdictional pipelines, and OSHA's process safety rule at 29 CFR 1910.119 applies to covered process units.

How the examination is performed

A thickness survey starts with a drawing or line list and a set of locations marked on the component, so future campaigns return to exactly the same spots. The technician cleans the surface, applies couplant, and calibrates on a step block of the same material, checking the calibration again during the job. Readings are logged by location, with probe, instrument and block recorded.

Cold weather changes the job. Ordinary gel couplant stiffens or freezes on a winter morning, and batteries lose capacity in the cold, so the procedure names a low-temperature couplant and the crew keeps instruments warm between readings. At the other extreme, hot process lines at a refinery need high-temperature probes and couplant plus a correction to the reading. Colorado's altitude does not change the physics of ultrasound, but wind, sun and rapid temperature swings do affect the work.

For welds, the technician builds a reference level from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, scans the weld from both sides where access allows, and evaluates each indication against the acceptance table, recording position, length and amplitude from a stated reference point.

Who does the examination and the review

Technicians are qualified under Atlantis's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Under that practice the employer certifies personnel. A Level II sets up, performs and interprets; an ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, fills that role. Owners who want procedures written, or their own written practice reviewed, can use Level III consulting and written practice development.

What the UT report contains

Each report names the component, line or tank, the drawing reference, the procedure number and revision, the code and edition, the instrument, probe, couplant and calibration block, and the technician and level. Thickness work produces a table or grid by location, showing nominal wall and required minimum where the owner provides them, and any reading below the threshold is flagged instead of buried. Weld work lists each reportable indication with its position, length and amplitude or depth, and the accept or reject call. Sketches show what was scanned and which areas were inaccessible, because a report that hides its gaps is worse than none.

Planning a UT job in Denver

Seasons set the plan. Winter work needs cold-rated couplant and instruments, and snow cover can hide piping and tank shells. Summer afternoon thunderstorms with hail and lightning stop exposed work with little warning, and strong sun can make surfaces hot enough for the high-temperature procedure. Travel across the Front Range and out to the basin sites may involve long drives, and mountain passes close in storms. Many oil and gas sites need safety orientation before entry, and refinery access normally needs badging, so names should go in early.

Atlantis has no office in Denver. Technicians travel to your site from outside the area for the agreed scope, with travel and lodging built into the quote.

Turning readings into decisions

A thickness reading becomes useful when it is compared with something. The owner's engineer or authorized inspector sets a required minimum wall, taking pressure, temperature, material and corrosion allowance into account, and the survey is judged against it. Between campaigns the readings give a corrosion rate. A short-term rate comes from the last two readings at a location, while a long-term rate uses the whole history, and the inspector looks at both to see whether corrosion is accelerating. From the rate and the margin above the required minimum, the owner derives remaining life and the next inspection date. Because that calculation depends on small differences in wall thickness, a change in technique, a different probe or a shifted location between campaigns can look like corrosion that is not there, or hide corrosion that is.

For that reason Atlantis records the technique details alongside each reading and tries to repeat them. The same condition monitoring location is read each time, with a permanent mark, a photograph or a sketch where the line is complex. If a reading looks out of line with history, the technician repeats it, checks the calibration, and examines the neighborhood with a scan before accepting the number. A suspicious area that spot readings cannot characterize may call for a closer grid of readings or a corrosion map, which the owner and the Level III discuss before the work is expanded.

Weld examination results follow a different path. The acceptance table in the code converts an indication's amplitude and length into accept or reject, and rejected welds go to the owner's repair process. After a repair, the weld is re-examined to the same procedure, and the report links the original and repeat examinations. Where a code allows engineering evaluation of a flaw, that evaluation is the owner's engineer's work and relies on accurate sizing data from the examination.

Colorado operators with flowline obligations have an additional reason to keep clean, consistent records. Regulators review pressure-test records and integrity data on registered lines, so an operator whose thickness data is traceable by line and location is better placed in an audit than one with scattered spreadsheets.

Scope changes are normal on outage and construction jobs. If additional lines or welds are added after the quote, tell us early so crew size, probes and calibration blocks match the real workload.

UT, MT or PT for your Denver job

Use UT for remaining wall and internal weld flaws. For surface cracks on carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in Denver is the faster tool, and for stainless steel, alloys or aluminum, liquid penetrant testing in Denver applies. Many shutdown scopes combine all three on the same vessel. The national ultrasonic testing page and the ultimate UT guide go further into the method, and the thickness measurement requirements article covers the standard.

Training your own UT technicians

Owners who want their own in-house technicians can use the UT Level 1 course and UT Level 2 course, practice on the Practical NDT UT simulator, and check eligibility through the SNT-TC-1A eligibility guide. Enrollment details for the metro are on the Denver NDT training page.

faq.q: Can you do ultrasonic thickness surveys on DJ Basin flowlines and gathering piping?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to the site, survey risers, bends and low points with dual-element probes, and report thickness by location so the operator's integrity group can compare results across campaigns.

faq.q: Does cold weather stop ultrasonic testing in Denver?
faq.a: Not usually. The procedure specifies a couplant rated for low temperatures, and crews keep instruments warm. Severe cold, ice or snow cover on equipment can still delay work, which is why dates stay flexible in winter.

faq.q: Which code governs UT of pipeline welds in Colorado?
faq.a: API 1104 governs pipeline welding and its ultrasonic provisions apply where the owner's procedure selects that method. Technique requirements come from ASME Section V Article 4, and PHMSA rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 apply to jurisdictional lines.

faq.q: Are Atlantis technicians API authorized inspectors?
faq.a: No. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection program. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and provides thickness data and indications for that inspector to evaluate.

faq.q: Can UT be used on mining equipment wear plates and mill shells?
faq.a: Yes. Thickness surveys on liners, chutes, plates and shells show remaining wear and help schedule replacement, and weld examination on structural parts such as booms follows AWS D1.1 acceptance where the owner specifies it.

faq.q: Does ultrasonic testing replace radiography on welds?
faq.a: Only where code and owner both permit it. The owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector agree before the job, and the contract names the acceptance criteria for the ultrasonic examination.

faq.q: What does the Colorado boiler program have to do with UT?
faq.a: The Division of Oil and Public Safety inspects boilers and some pressure vessels in commercial and public buildings. Owners sometimes request thickness data as supporting evidence for those inspections or for repairs.

faq.q: What do you need to quote a Denver UT job?
faq.a: Send drawings or line lists, materials and nominal wall, the locations or welds to be examined, the code and edition, temperatures, access needs and dates. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can you train our staff to do UT in-house?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and Level 2 training and a simulator for practice, and your company qualifies and certifies its own staff under its written practice. We can review that written practice too.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Denver, CO
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection and MT testing for Denver area mining equipment, refinery welds, cranes and steel fabrication, on your site. Request MPI quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Denver, Colorado
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection on carbon and low-alloy steel for Denver-area owners: weld toes and repair excavations at refineries and processing plants, structural and lifting steel on mining and aggregate equipment, crane and rigging components, and fabricated steel at metal shops. Technicians are mobilized to your site with yokes, particles and light meters, work to a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request a mag particle quote for your Denver site and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used around Denver

The Front Range economy is built on heavy steel that works hard: gathering and compression facilities for the basin's oil and gas production, process equipment at the Commerce City refinery, mining and quarrying machines that run through the mountain states, and a metro-area fabrication base. These are fatigue environments. Moving parts, cyclic loading, wind and thermal swings concentrate stress at welds and attachments, and cracks start at the surface where a magnetic method sees them best.

Examples of MT work in this market:

  • Weld toes and repair excavations on piping and vessels at the refinery, checked before welding resumes.
  • Compressor station skids, pulsation bottle supports and pipe supports, where vibration fatigues welds.
  • Dragline booms, shovel frames, haul-truck structures and crusher frames on mining and aggregate equipment.
  • Lifting lugs, hooks, shackles and spreader beams used for rigging on construction and plant sites.
  • Structural steel connections on buildings, platforms and crane runways in the metro area.
  • Gears, shafts and other ferromagnetic machined parts during rebuilds at shops.

What magnetic particle inspection finds, and what it misses

Magnetizing a steel part causes any surface-breaking or near-surface discontinuity to leak flux into the air above it, and iron particles collect there as a visible line. The method applies only to ferromagnetic materials, so carbon steel and most alloy steels qualify but austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper do not. Sensitivity drops rapidly with depth, so deep internal flaws pass unseen, and the method cannot say anything about remaining wall.

Two practical points decide whether an examination is good. First, field direction: a crack parallel to the magnetic field produces almost no leakage, so a second pass at roughly right angles is required. Second, surface condition: scale, rust, grease and thick paint block the field or hold particles in the wrong places. Geometry also produces non-relevant indications, for example at a sharp change of section, and the technician has to recognize those and keep them out of the reject list. Dry Colorado air is a mild advantage here, as dry particles move freely on a dry surface, but static and wind can disturb powder at the edge of a weld.

Codes and Colorado context

Technique comes from ASME Section V Article 7, supported by ASTM E709 and ASTM E1444. For vessels, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 6 provides methods and acceptance. Process piping follows ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 with the acceptance limits in Table 341.3.2, and structural welds follow AWS D1.1, while state steel bridges may follow AWS D1.5.

In-service work falls under API 510, 570 and 653 with the owner's authorized inspector responsible; Atlantis performs the examination and supplies the report and is not inspector of record. Colorado's Division of Oil and Public Safety, part of the Department of Labor and Employment, runs the state boiler inspection program for boilers and some pressure vessels in commercial and public buildings, using state inspectors or commissioned insurance company inspectors. For oil and gas, the Energy and Carbon Management Commission's flowline rules cover lines from the wellhead to facilities, and its integrity staff review flowline systems; where an operator needs weld repairs verified on those lines, a surface examination report is a common supporting record.

Technique in the field

Most field MT uses an electromagnetic yoke. ASME Section V Article 7 sets minimum lifting power of 10 pounds for an alternating-current yoke at the maximum pole spacing used, and 40 pounds for a direct-current or permanent-magnet yoke, and the technician proves this on a test weight at the start of the job. The weld and adjacent base metal are cleaned. Particles, dry powder or wet visible suspension, are applied while the yoke is energized, and the examination is repeated with the yoke rotated about 90 degrees.

Where greater sensitivity is required, wet fluorescent particles are examined under ultraviolet light in darkness, and ambient white light is kept below the limit stated in the Article, so the work is arranged in a shop, a tent or an enclosure. Altitude puts the sun high and the sky bright, and outdoor fluorescent work in midday is difficult without a shelter. Indications are marked, measured and photographed. Demagnetization follows when residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining or service. Cold also affects wet methods: bath carriers can thicken, and the procedure states the minimum surface temperature at which the chosen material works.

Who does the work

Magnetic particle technicians are qualified under Atlantis's written practice following ASNT SNT-TC-1A, under which the employer certifies personnel. A Level II performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, is the company's Level III. Owners can ask for a review of their MT procedure through Level III consulting, or for a written practice through written practice development.

What the MT report contains

The report lists the part or weld, drawing or line reference, procedure and revision, code and edition, equipment including the yoke lifting-power check, particle type and color, light-meter readings where they apply, the surface condition, the technician and level, and the date. Each indication is described by position, orientation and length, with photographs where helpful, and receives an accept or reject call under the acceptance criteria in the contract. Areas that could not be examined, such as a weld behind a bracket, are listed. When demagnetization is done, the report says so and records the check.

Planning an MT job in Denver

Weather can interrupt exposed MT work. Winter cold limits particle carriers and operator dexterity, wind blows powder away, and snow or frost on steel keeps particles from adhering. Summer storms bring lightning that clears sites with little notice. Sun glare reduces the contrast of visible particles, so contrast paint or shading is common. Remote sites in the basin or mountains add driving time, and some operations require safety orientation before entry. Enclosed vessel entry adds confined-space permits.

Atlantis does not maintain an office in Denver. Technicians are mobilized to your site, and travel and lodging are planned into the quote.

Problems that spoil a magnetic particle examination

Several things can compromise an MT result, and field crews on the Front Range meet most of them. A yoke that is too weak for the pole spacing leaves the field too low to hold particles. Rough weld surfaces, scale and grease hold powder in the wrong places or keep it from moving. Wind scatters dry powder before it can settle, so shielding the work area with a screen is routine. Freezing temperatures thicken wet carriers, and cold steel can have a film of frost that stops particles sticking, so surfaces are cleaned and dried before the yoke is energized.

Contrast is a frequent issue at altitude. Bright sky and strong sun wash out the visibility of dark particles on bare steel, and a thin layer of white contrast paint, kept within the thickness the procedure was demonstrated on, restores the picture. For fluorescent work the opposite is needed: darkness. A shop bay, a tarp tent or a vessel interior gives a dark area, and the ultraviolet lamp's intensity at the surface and the ambient white light level are measured with calibrated meters and written in the report.

Field direction deserves the most attention. With a yoke, the field runs between the legs, so a crack along that line is nearly invisible. The second pass at right angles solves that problem, and for complex shapes like nozzle junctions or lugs, extra positions are used so no part of the weld is missed. The technician also watches for false trails: a magnetic writing effect from a screwdriver or a prior contact point, particle build-up along a sharp toe, or a change of section can each look like a crack. A Level II decides by re-examining after demagnetizing.

Residual magnetism after the job can attract chips, disturb welding and interfere with instruments. When the procedure requires it, the part is demagnetized and the field checked. On mining equipment, demagnetization is often called for on shafts, gears and bearing seats before reassembly.

Finally, coatings: owners often ask whether the examination can be done through paint. Thin, tightly adherent coatings can sometimes be examined if the procedure was demonstrated that way, but thick paint reduces sensitivity. Stripping at the weld is the safer path, and re-coating afterward is recorded as an owner responsibility.

Wet suspensions bring a further point for cold climates: the bath concentration is checked with a settling test at the start of a job and again when the fluid has been in use for some time, because carrier loss and temperature swings change particle density. A bath that is too thin misses fine cracks and one that is too thick leaves a heavy background, so the check is written into the record next to the batch details.

Share weld maps or equipment lists before mobilization so the crew arrives with the right yokes, particles, contrast paint and lights for the actual steel rather than a generic kit.

MT, PT or UT for your Denver job

Magnetic particle inspection is the usual first choice for surface cracks in carbon steel welds. When the part is stainless, aluminum or another non-magnetic alloy, use liquid penetrant testing in Denver. When the question is internal flaws or wall loss, use ultrasonic testing in Denver. See the national magnetic particle testing page and the complete MT guide, and the Article 7 explainer for the standard.

Training your own MT technicians

If you would rather build in-house capability, start with MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 training, and practice with the NDT practice tests. Local enrollment details are on the Denver NDT training page.

faq.q: What can magnetic particle inspection examine on mining and aggregate equipment?
faq.a: Frames, booms, buckets, crusher structures, shafts and gears made of ferromagnetic steel. The method finds surface and near-surface cracks that grow from fatigue, which is common on equipment working under cyclic load.

faq.q: Can MT be done outdoors in Denver winters?
faq.a: Often yes, with a procedure that states the minimum surface temperature for the particles and carrier. Frost and snow on the steel prevent particles from adhering, so surfaces must be cleaned and dry, and severe cold can delay work.

faq.q: Why does the yoke have to be tested at the start of a job?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 7 requires a minimum lifting power, 10 pounds for alternating-current yokes and 40 pounds for direct-current or permanent-magnet yokes, at the maximum pole spacing. A test weight shows the yoke is strong enough.

faq.q: Does magnetic particle inspection work on stainless steel pipe?
faq.a: Not on austenitic stainless steel, which is not ferromagnetic. For stainless piping and welds, liquid penetrant testing is used to find surface-breaking cracks and porosity instead of magnetic particles.

faq.q: Do you do wet fluorescent MT in Denver?
faq.a: Yes, when the specification calls for higher sensitivity. It needs ultraviolet light and a darkened area, so we plan it for a shop, tent or enclosure, with the light intensity and ambient light limits checked and recorded.

faq.q: Which standard sets MT acceptance for pressure vessels?
faq.a: For vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1, Mandatory Appendix 6 provides methods and acceptance. Piping uses ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2, and structural steel uses AWS D1.1, depending on the construction code named in the contract.

faq.q: Is Atlantis an API authorized inspector for Denver refineries?
faq.a: No. The owner's authorized inspector is responsible under API 510, 570 and 653. Atlantis performs the magnetic particle examination and gives that inspector a report with indications, equipment records and the procedure.

faq.q: What do I send to request an MT quote in Denver?
faq.a: Send equipment or weld lists, materials, the governing code and edition, surface condition, site access requirements and dates. We reply within one business day and confirm the scope and mobilization plan.

faq.q: Can you review or write our MT procedure?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT NDT Level III can prepare or review a magnetic particle procedure against ASME Section V Article 7 and your construction code, and review the written practice behind your technicians' qualifications.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Denver, CO
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection for Denver area stainless, aluminum and alloy welds, parts and repairs, on your site. Request PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Denver, Colorado
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection for Denver-area owners on stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and other non-magnetic materials, as well as on carbon steel where magnetic particle testing is impractical. Typical scopes include welds on process piping, machined and rebuilt parts, repair excavations and fabricated assemblies. Technicians are mobilized to your site with materials matched to the alloy, work to a written procedure, and report against the code you name. Request a penetrant quote for your Denver site and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used around Denver

The metro area's work is varied, and much of it involves metals that magnetic methods cannot examine. Refinery and processing plants have stainless and alloy piping and overlay. Machine shops and equipment manufacturers rebuild shafts, valve bodies and housings. Colorado is known for brewing and food production, which rely on stainless steel vessels and sanitary piping welded to high surface standards. Aerospace and defense suppliers along the Front Range machine aluminum, titanium and steel components where surface cracks are rejectable. Mining and power equipment have non-magnetic manganese and alloy parts.

Examples include:

  • Stainless and nickel alloy pipe welds, branch connections and repair excavations in process plants.
  • Stainless vessels, jacketed tanks and heat exchanger tubesheet welds in processing facilities.
  • Aluminum and titanium fabrications and machined parts in manufacturing.
  • Valve bodies, pump casings, shafts and seal faces during rebuilds.
  • Austenitic manganese wear components and hardfacing repairs on mining equipment.
  • Excavations in any material, to prove a defect has been completely removed.

What penetrant testing finds, and what it misses

Penetrant examination detects discontinuities that are open to the surface. A thin liquid is applied, enters any crack, lap or pore by capillary action, and after excess is cleaned away a developer pulls it back out so the flaw shows as a line or dot. The liquid is either a colored dye seen in white light or a fluorescent type seen under ultraviolet light. The method works on any non-porous material, ferrous or not.

It misses what does not reach the surface: buried lack of fusion, internal porosity and subsurface cracks, all of which need ultrasonic testing. It also misses flaws that are blocked, whether by smeared metal from grinding or peening, by paint, oil or scale in the opening, or by a surface too rough to clean. It gives no depth. Colorado's low humidity and strong sun add a particular risk: penetrant and cleaner evaporate faster, and a film that dries during the dwell will not draw back out of a fine crack, so the technician controls dwell on the surface rather than trusting the clock alone.

Codes, materials and Colorado oversight

Technique comes from ASME Section V Article 6, along with ASTM E165 for general industry and ASTM E1417 for fluorescent processes called out in some specifications. For pressure vessels, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 8 provides methods and acceptance. Piping under ASME B31.3 uses paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2, and stainless fabrications may reference AWS D1.6 alongside AWS D1.1 for structures.

Material controls matter on the alloys common here. For austenitic stainless and nickel-base alloys, Article 6 limits sulfur and halogen content of the penetrant materials, and batch certificates stay with the record. Residues are cleaned afterward so chlorides do not remain on stainless surfaces. For in-service equipment under API 510, 570 and 653, the owner's authorized inspector is responsible, and Atlantis provides examination data without acting as inspector of record. Colorado's boiler program, run by the Division of Oil and Public Safety within the Department of Labor and Employment, covers boilers and some pressure vessels in commercial and public buildings, using state or commissioned insurance inspectors. Workplace safety at process sites is enforced by federal OSHA.

Technique, step by step

The procedure names the penetrant family and removal method. Fluorescent penetrant is Type I and visible dye is Type II; removal is by water wash, lipophilic or hydrophilic emulsifier, or solvent wipe. For field work on installed piping, visible dye with solvent removal and a solvent-suspended developer is typical because no water or darkness is needed. Shop work on production parts may use fluorescent penetrant with dry powder developer in a booth.

The sequence: clean and dry the surface, apply penetrant by spray or brush, hold the dwell time stated in the procedure, remove excess with a cloth lightly dampened with solvent rather than a direct spray, apply a thin even coat of developer, wait the development time, and examine under suitable light. Indications are recorded quickly because bleed-out spreads.

Temperature is a defined limit. Article 6 sets 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, about 5 to 52 degrees Celsius, as the standard range for the part and materials. Outside it the procedure must be qualified for the temperature, and Denver winters regularly fall below the lower end, so cold-weather jobs are either warmed or covered by a qualified procedure.

Who performs and approves the work

Penetrant technicians work under Atlantis's written practice following ASNT SNT-TC-1A, in which the employer certifies personnel. A Level II performs and evaluates the examination, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, serves as the company's Level III. A plant that needs a PT procedure written for a particular alloy, outdoor dwell control or low temperatures can use Level III consulting and written practice development.

What the PT report contains

The report identifies the part or weld, drawing reference, material and finish, procedure and revision, code and edition, penetrant, remover and developer by brand and batch, sulfur and halogen certification where required, cleaning method, dwell and development times, surface temperature, light conditions, and the technician and level. Relevant indications are described by location, shape and size with photographs or sketches and an accept or reject call. Non-relevant indications are noted with reasons. Post-examination cleaning is recorded so the owner knows the surface was left clean and ready for service or coating.

Planning a PT job in Denver

Denver conditions change the plan. Dry air and sun speed evaporation, so work is shaded and divided into small areas that can be finished before the film dries. Wind blows overspray and dust onto wet surfaces. Cold mornings can push surfaces below 40 degrees. Afternoon storms may arrive with hail and lightning. Dust from construction and mining sites can contaminate surfaces, and the final cleaning stage needs care to leave a clean part. Travel to basin or mountain sites can be long, and safety orientation is common at industrial sites.

Atlantis has no office in Denver. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, with materials carried or shipped and travel planned into the quote.

Problems that spoil a penetrant examination

Penetrant work fails quietly: a poor examination can look exactly like a clean one. The biggest cause is inadequate pre-cleaning. Oil, machining coolant, paint, weld flux and dust from construction or mining sites can block crack mouths, and a surface that looks clean may still return no indications. A suitable solvent is selected for the contaminant, and the surface is allowed to dry fully because cleaner trapped in a flaw dilutes the penetrant.

The second problem is mechanical closing of flaws. Grinding, wire brushing, shot blasting and peening can smear metal over the opening of a crack. Procedures restrict those operations before penetrant testing on critical parts, and a chemical etch followed by cleaning may be specified when smearing is suspected, particularly on soft metals such as aluminum and on machined surfaces.

Dwell and removal are the third. Too short a dwell leaves tight cracks unfilled. In dry mountain air a long dwell can dry the film. The remedy is shading, reapplying penetrant during dwell and working in manageable sections. Excess removal has to be thorough without being aggressive: wiping with a solvent-dampened cloth removes surface penetrant, while spraying solvent directly onto the part can flush shallow flaws. For water-washable and emulsified systems, the wash is controlled for pressure, temperature and time.

Developer application is the fourth. A heavy, patchy coat hides fine indications and a thin one draws too little penetrant. Technicians apply it in a thin, even layer from the specified distance and wait for the development time before reading. Indications are watched as they develop, because their growth over the first minutes helps distinguish a tight crack from a wide pore.

False indications arise from weld ripples, tool marks and penetrant trapped in surface roughness, and from fingerprints or lint. Technicians re-clean and re-develop to see whether a mark returns in the same spot. Work in Denver also has to account for wind carrying dust onto wet surfaces and for cold mornings that bring surfaces below the standard temperature range. Documented procedures, material certificates and a Level III review of unusual alloys keep the result defensible.

One more field habit helps. Before the live examination, technicians often run the process on a known reference part or a test panel with real cracks, which shows the penetrant, remover and developer are working under that day's temperature and wind. If the panel shows its cracks, the work proceeds; if not, the materials or the method are adjusted first, and the check is noted in the report.

Share the alloy list and expected surface temperatures before mobilization, so the crew arrives with the right penetrant family, cleaners and developer rather than a generic kit. Where parts are going to be coated or anodized afterward, mention it too, because the final cleaning step is then planned around the finish.

PT, MT or UT for your Denver job

If the part is stainless steel, aluminum, titanium or any non-magnetic alloy, penetrant testing is the surface method that works. On carbon steel welds, magnetic particle inspection in Denver is usually quicker and also reveals slightly subsurface flaws. For internal flaws and remaining wall, ultrasonic testing in Denver is the right choice. The national penetrant testing page explains the method more broadly, and the MT versus PT comparison helps decide between surface methods.

Training your own PT technicians

Companies that want in-house capability can begin with PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 training, practice on the Practical NDT penetrant simulator, and see enrollment for the metro on the Denver NDT training page.

faq.q: Why does dry Colorado air matter for penetrant testing?
faq.a: Low humidity and strong sun make penetrant and cleaner evaporate quickly. A penetrant that dries during dwell will not draw back out of a fine crack, so work is shaded, done in small sections and kept wet.

faq.q: Can liquid penetrant testing be done below 40 degrees Fahrenheit?
faq.a: Only under a procedure qualified for that temperature. ASME Section V Article 6 sets 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit as the standard range, so Denver winter work is warmed, enclosed or covered by a qualified low-temperature procedure.

faq.q: Which metals can be examined with dye penetrant?
faq.a: Any non-porous metal, including stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, nickel alloys, copper alloys and carbon steel. It is the standard surface method for materials that cannot be magnetized, such as austenitic stainless steel and aluminum.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing find cracks beneath the surface?
faq.a: No. It detects only flaws open to the surface. Subsurface cracks, internal porosity and buried lack of fusion require ultrasonic testing, which examines the volume of the weld or part.

faq.q: What is the difference between Type I and Type II penetrant?
faq.a: Type I is fluorescent and examined under ultraviolet light, giving high sensitivity in a darkened area. Type II is visible dye examined in white light, which is practical for field work on installed piping.

faq.q: Are special penetrant materials required for stainless steel?
faq.a: Yes. ASME Section V Article 6 restricts sulfur and halogen content in penetrant materials used on austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys, and the batch certificates are kept with the report.

faq.q: Is Atlantis the authorized inspector for API 510 or 570 work?
faq.a: No. Under those documents the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the program, while Atlantis performs the penetrant examination and gives that inspector the report, procedure and materials records.

faq.q: What should I send to request a PT quote in Denver?
faq.a: Send the parts or welds, materials and surface finish, governing code and edition, expected temperatures, cleaning restrictions, access rules and dates. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can Atlantis write a penetrant procedure for outdoor or cold-weather work?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT NDT Level III can prepare or review a procedure to ASME Section V Article 6 covering dwell control, temperature limits, alloy material controls and cleaning for your site conditions.

rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. See UT alternatives, Level III radiograph review and RT theory training for Denver owners. Ask for a quote.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing in Denver, Colorado: What Atlantis Offers
rt.html:
If you are looking for radiographic testing in Denver, here is the plain answer: Atlantis does not carry out radiographic examination anywhere in the United States. Industrial radiography here is a licensed activity under NRC rules in 10 CFR Part 34 or the equivalent rules of Agreement States, and Colorado is an Agreement State. It is not a service Atlantis offers here, and we do not name or recommend radiography contractors. There are still useful things we do for a Denver owner who started with that search: ultrasonic examination where the code allows it, Level III review of radiographic records, and theory training. Describe your Denver scope and we reply within one business day.

Ultrasonic testing as the volumetric option

Both radiography and ultrasonic testing look inside a weld. Several codes make room for UT: ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain ultrasonic examination provisions for production welds, AWS D1.1 sets ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII Division 1 allows UT in place of radiography only under specific conditions. Substitution is never automatic. It must be agreed with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job begins, and the contract must state the acceptance criteria.

When that agreement is in place, Atlantis technicians are mobilized to your Denver-area site and examine welds with shear-wave technique to a written procedure based on ASME Section V Article 4. The practical benefit is that no exclusion zone is needed, so other trades can keep working on a crowded pipe rack or in a fabrication shop. UT does not leave a film or image record, and it responds differently to flaw orientation, so the decision should be made with the engineer. Details are on the ultrasonic testing service in Denver page.

Level III review of radiographs and procedures

Reviewing existing radiographs does not involve handling a source, so no radiation licence is needed. An ASNT NDT Level III can read film or digital images supplied by your radiography contractor, examine technique sheets, image quality indicators and density against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, and give a second read where an indication is disputed. The same Level III can review a radiography contractor's procedure and written practice, and the way records are kept. Owners use this on pipeline tie-ins, refinery repairs and fabricated pressure equipment when they want an independent view before accepting a weld. Anoop Rayavarapu, Atlantis's founder, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. See Level III consulting.

Other conventional methods offered in Denver

For surface cracks, Atlantis performs magnetic particle inspection on ferromagnetic steel and liquid penetrant testing on non-magnetic alloys and other materials.

Radiography theory training

People who want to understand the method can take the radiographic testing Level 2 course, which teaches the theory. Radiation safety and source handling are regulated separately, and a course does not replace licensing or the employer's qualification under its written practice. Enrollment for the metro is on the Denver NDT training page.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in Denver?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not provide radiography in the United States. The work is licensed under NRC rules in 10 CFR Part 34 or the equivalent rules of Agreement States such as Colorado, and we do not offer it.

faq.q: Is ultrasonic testing accepted instead of radiography?
faq.a: Only when code and owner both permit it. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 contain UT provisions, and Section VIII Division 1 permits it under conditions, but all parties must agree beforehand.

faq.q: Can you review radiographs from my radiography contractor?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT NDT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, and provide a second read on disputed indications.

faq.q: Can a Level III review a radiography procedure?
faq.a: Yes. The review compares the procedure with the code and contract, checks the written practice and qualification records, and reports gaps. It is a document review and involves no radioactive source.

faq.q: Will you recommend a radiography contractor in Denver?
faq.a: No. We do not name or recommend radiography contractors. Owners select a licensed provider, and we can support the quality side with independent review or with ultrasonic examination where the code allows.

faq.q: Does Atlantis teach radiography?
faq.a: A Level 2 radiographic testing course from Atlantis covers theory only. Radiation safety certification and source handling are separate regulated requirements, and each employer qualifies its own personnel.
